sections.note: 12 paired statements. Consistency is the signal.

debug.prompt: This should return the maximum subarray sum. It returns the wrong answer for all-negative arrays.
options: Line 2: `best` should be initialised to `a[0]`, not `0`
The loop should start from index 1
debug.explain: Initialising best to 0 means an all-negative array returns 0, which is not a valid subarray sum. Initialise best = a[0] (and cur = a[0], looping from index 1) so at least one element is always taken.

debug.prompt: Binary search that should return the index of target, or -1. It infinite-loops on some inputs.
options: Lines 6 and 7: should be `lo = mid + 1` and `hi = mid - 1`
debug.explain: Without the +1 / -1 the window never shrinks when hi = lo + 1, so the loop spins forever. Overflow in (lo+hi)/2 is a real secondary issue — lo + (hi-lo)/2 is safer — but it does not cause the infinite loop.

debug.prompt: Should count vowels in a string. Always returns 0.
options: Line 5: the condition is inverted — should be `!= -1`
debug.explain: indexOf returns -1 when the char is NOT found. The condition counts consonants. It returns 0 only for all-vowel strings, but the logical bug is the inverted comparison.

debug.prompt: Should reverse a linked list. Returns only the last node.
options: Line 7: should be `cur = next` — `cur.next` was just overwritten
debug.explain: Line 5 already reassigned cur.next to prev, so line 7 walks backwards. Use the saved `next` reference.

debug.prompt: Should return true if the array contains a duplicate. Returns false for [1,1].
options: Line 4 and 5 are in the wrong order — check membership before adding
debug.explain: Adding first guarantees contains() is always true, so it always continues. Check `if (!seen.add(v)) return true;` — add() returns false when the element was already present.

debug.prompt: Should compute n! for n >= 0. StackOverflowError for n = 0.
debug.explain: With n = 0 it recurses to -1, -2, ... forever. `n <= 1` (or n == 0) terminates correctly. Overflow past n = 20 is a real but separate concern.

debug.prompt: Should remove all occurrences of a value from a list. Skips some elements.
options: Line 4: `remove(i)` shifts elements left, so `i` must be decremented after removal
debug.explain: After removing index i, the next element slides into position i but the loop increments past it. Fix with i-- after removal, or iterate backwards, or use an Iterator. Note: remove(int) vs remove(Object) is also a classic Java trap with boxed Integers.

coding.title: Minimum Array Operations
coding.statement:
Given an integer array arr, you may pick an index i and a value x where -10 <= x <= 10, and set arr[i] = x. Modify the array so that the sum of every subarray of length greater than 1 is non-negative. Return the minimum number of operations required.

Example:
arr = [2, 5, -3, -1, 2]  ->  1
Setting index 2 to 10 gives [2, 5, 10, -1, 2], where every subarray of length > 1 has a non-negative sum.

Constraints: 1 <= arr.length <= 10^5, -10^9 <= arr[i] <= 10^9
coding.hint: Track a running cumulative sum. What must be true the moment it dips below zero?
coding.approach: Prefix sum with state reset. Walk the array accumulating a running sum. Whenever the running sum goes negative, that prefix already violates the constraint — count one operation and reset the running sum to 0. Any violating window must pass through such a dip, and repairing at the earliest dip lifts every window through that point.

coding.title: Server Allocation Cost
coding.statement:
You are given an array servers, where index i is a server ID and servers[i] is the number of idle instances on it. m customers arrive one at a time. Each customer picks the server with the most idle instances and rents exactly one instance from it. The cost charged to that customer is (max_instances + min_instances), where both values are measured across all servers BEFORE that customer's selection. After all m customers, return the total cumulative cost.

Example:
servers = [3, 1, 4], m = 3
Customer 1: max=4, min=1 -> cost 5. servers becomes [3,1,3]
Customer 2: max=3, min=1 -> cost 4. servers becomes [3,1,2]
Customer 3: max=3, min=1 -> cost 4.
Total = 13

Constraints: 1 <= servers.length <= 10^5, 1 <= m <= 10^5
coding.hint: You need the maximum and the minimum of a changing multiset, quickly. What structure gives you both ends in log n?
coding.approach: Use a TreeMap<Integer,Integer> as a multiset: firstKey() is the min, lastKey() is the max, both O(log n). Read cost before mutating, then decrement the chosen max and reinsert. A dual max-heap/min-heap works too but requires lazy deletion to stay in sync, which is a common source of bugs — mention that trade-off out loud.
coding.complexity: O(m log n) time, O(n) space

corecs.q: A process executes `fork()` three times sequentially. How many processes exist in total, including the original?
corecs.explain: Each fork doubles the process count: 2^3 = 8 total.

corecs.q: Which is NOT one of the four Coffman conditions for deadlock?
corecs.explain: The fourth condition is NO preemption. Allowing preemption breaks deadlock.

corecs.q: Reference string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5 with 3 frames using FIFO. How many page faults?
corecs.explain: 1,2,3 fault (3). 4 evicts 1 (4). 1 evicts 2 (5). 2 evicts 3 (6). 5 evicts 4 (7). Total 7.

corecs.q: A semaphore initialised to 3 allows how many processes into the critical section concurrently?
corecs.explain: A counting semaphore initialised to N permits N concurrent entries. Initialised to 1 it is a binary semaphore/mutex.

corecs.q: `chmod 640 file.txt` gives which permissions?
corecs.explain: 6 = rw- (owner), 4 = r-- (group), 0 = --- (others).

corecs.q: Which command prints the number of lines in file.log containing the word ERROR?
corecs.explain: -c counts matching lines. -n prefixes line numbers instead of counting.

corecs.q: What is the difference between a hard link and a symbolic link?
options: A hard link points to the same inode; a symlink stores a path and breaks if the target moves
A symlink points to the same inode; a hard link stores a path
Hard links only work across filesystems
corecs.explain: Hard links share the inode and survive renames of the original. Symlinks store a path and dangle if the target is removed. Hard links cannot cross filesystems.

corecs.q: `2>&1` in a shell command does what?
corecs.explain: It duplicates fd 2 (stderr) onto fd 1 (stdout), so both flow to the same destination.

corecs.q: A relation has FDs A -> B and B -> C, with A as the primary key. What is the highest normal form it satisfies?
corecs.explain: A -> B -> C is a transitive dependency on the key, which violates 3NF. It is in 2NF.

corecs.q: Which isolation level prevents dirty reads and non-repeatable reads but still allows phantom reads?
corecs.explain: REPEATABLE READ locks rows already read but not ranges, so newly inserted rows matching the predicate can still appear.

corecs.q: Table A has 5 rows, Table B has 3 rows. How many rows does `SELECT * FROM A CROSS JOIN B` return?
corecs.explain: A cross join is the Cartesian product: 5 x 3 = 15.

corecs.q: Which is true of WHERE vs HAVING?
options: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation
WHERE cannot be used with GROUP BY
corecs.explain: WHERE applies to individual rows pre-aggregation. HAVING applies to aggregate results post-GROUP BY.

corecs.q: Worst-case time complexity of quicksort, and when it occurs?
options: O(n^2), when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element
O(n^2), when the array is random
corecs.explain: A maximally unbalanced partition at every level gives O(n^2). Sorted input with a first-element pivot triggers it.

corecs.q: Solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n using the Master theorem.
corecs.explain: a=2, b=2, so n^(log_b a) = n. f(n) = n matches, giving Case 2: O(n log n).

corecs.q: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm fail on graphs with negative edge weights?
options: Once a node is finalised it is never revisited, but a negative edge could later offer a shorter path
corecs.explain: Dijkstra's greedy invariant assumes distances only grow as you extend a path. Negative edges break that, so use Bellman-Ford.

corecs.q: Which structure gives O(1) average lookup but O(n) worst case?
corecs.explain: With every key colliding into one bucket, a hash table degenerates to a linked-list scan. Java 8+ converts long buckets to trees, softening this to O(log n).

corecs.q: What does `new Integer(127) == new Integer(127)` evaluate to?
corecs.explain: `new` forces distinct objects, so reference comparison is false. Note that `Integer a = 127; Integer b = 127; a == b` IS true due to the Integer cache for -128..127.

corecs.q: Which collection maintains insertion order AND allows O(1) average lookup by key?
corecs.explain: LinkedHashMap keeps a doubly-linked list across entries for predictable iteration order while retaining hash lookup.

corecs.q: A method has a `return` in `try` and a `return` in `finally`. Which wins?
corecs.explain: The finally block's return overrides and discards the try block's value. This is a well-known anti-pattern.

corecs.q: Which is a checked exception?
corecs.explain: IOException extends Exception and must be declared or caught. The others extend RuntimeException and are unchecked.

reasoning.q: If one program solves a problem of size N in X steps, and the algorithm is O(N^2), roughly how many steps for size 2N?
reasoning.explain: Quadratic growth: doubling the input quadruples the work.

reasoning.q: All engineers are problem solvers. Some problem solvers are designers. Which necessarily follows?
options: No valid conclusion about engineers and designers
reasoning.explain: The overlap between problem solvers and designers may fall entirely outside the engineer subset, so nothing necessarily follows.

reasoning.q: A is B's father. C is B's sister. D is C's mother. How is D related to A?
reasoning.explain: C and B share parents. D is their mother; A is their father. D is A's wife.

reasoning.q: A server processes 240 requests in 4 minutes. Three identical servers process how many in 90 seconds?
reasoning.explain: One server: 60 req/min. Three: 180 req/min. In 1.5 min: 270.

reasoning.q: Facing north, you turn 90 degrees right, then 180 degrees, then 90 degrees left. Which way are you facing?
reasoning.explain: North, turn right 90 = East. Turn 180 = West. Turn left 90 from West = South.

reasoning.q: In a code, AMAZON is written as BNBAPO. How is CLOUD written?
reasoning.explain: Each letter shifts +1. C->D, L->M, O->P, U->V, D->E = DMPVE.

reasoning.q: Deploys succeed 80% of the time. Two independent deploys. Probability both succeed?
Five servers S1..S5 are in a rack. S3 is directly above S1. S5 is at the bottom. S2 is directly above S3. Which is at the top?
reasoning.explain: Bottom to top: S5, S1, S3, S2, leaving S4 at the top.

reasoning.q: A cache hit costs 2ms, a miss costs 50ms. With a 90% hit rate, what is the average latency?

worksim.scenario: It is 4pm Friday. A monitoring alert shows 3% of checkout requests are failing with a 500 error. You have not touched that service. Your own feature is due Monday. What do you do first?
options: Finish your feature — the checkout service belongs to another team
Check the error logs and recent deploys yourself, then post the specific finding in the team channel and flag the customer impact
Immediately page your manager and wait for direction
Post 'checkout looks broken?' in the channel and go back to your feature
worksim.explain: Ownership plus Dive Deep. You gather evidence first so your escalation is actionable, and you surface customer impact rather than saying 'not my job'. Option 2 is passive; option 0 is the classic ownership failure; option 3 escalates with no information.

worksim.scenario: Your tech lead chose a caching approach you believe will not scale. You have benchmark data suggesting a problem at 10x load. The decision meeting is tomorrow.
options: Stay quiet — you are an intern and the lead has more context
Raise it in the meeting with your benchmark data, ask what you might be missing, and if the decision stands, commit fully and help implement it
Email skip-level leadership about the concern
Implement it your own way and show it works later
worksim.explain: Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit, done correctly: evidence-based, respectful, in the right forum, and with genuine commitment afterwards. Option 0 lacks backbone; option 2 skips the chain; option 3 is disagree-and-defy.

worksim.scenario: You shipped a change that silently broke a report used by an ops team. You notice it two days later. Nobody else has flagged it.
options: Quietly fix it and say nothing since nobody noticed
Fix it, then tell your manager and the ops team what broke, for how long, what data was affected, and what guardrail you are adding
Wait to see if the ops team complains first
Fix it and mention it casually in standup weeks later
worksim.explain: Ownership and Earn Trust require being vocally self-critical. Disclosing scope and duration lets the ops team assess whether they made decisions on bad data — that is the customer impact.

worksim.scenario: You have five things in your inbox: a customer-facing bug affecting orders, a teammate asking for a code review, your manager requesting a status update, a meeting starting in 10 minutes, and a request to update documentation.
options: Handle them in the order they arrived
Triage the customer bug first, send a one-line ack to the review and status requests with an ETA, join the meeting, and defer the docs
Do the quick items first to clear the inbox, then the bug
Ask your manager to prioritise for you
worksim.explain: Customer Obsession sets the order, but strong answers also acknowledge the others rather than dropping them silently. Clearing quick wins while customers are impacted is the wrong instinct.

worksim.scenario: A metric dashboard says feature adoption is 40%. A teammate insists from user calls that 'almost nobody uses it'. Which is your next move?
options: Trust the dashboard — data beats anecdote
Trust the teammate — they talk to users
Verify the metric definition and query yourself, and check whether 'adoption' counts something different from active use
Escalate to the PM to decide
worksim.explain: Dive Deep explicitly says leaders are skeptical when metrics and anecdote differ. Usually the metric definition is the culprit — e.g. counting one-time visits as adoption.

worksim.scenario: You are two days from a deadline and realise the proper fix needs a week. A hack would work but leaves a known edge case that could corrupt a small number of records.
options: Ship the hack and file a follow-up ticket
Ship the hack silently to hit the date
Flag it now with the specific risk and record volume, propose either a scoped-down safe release or a short slip, and let the decision be made with full information
Miss the deadline without telling anyone until the day
worksim.explain: Insist on the Highest Standards says defects must not get sent down the line. Data corruption is not an acceptable trade for a date, but the strong answer is transparent escalation with options, not a unilateral call.

worksim.scenario: A new intern on your team is struggling with the codebase and is falling behind, but has not asked for help.
options: Stay out of it — their mentor's job
Offer a short pairing session, share the mental model of how the service fits together, and point them at the two docs that unblocked you
Report the concern to their manager
Do part of their task for them so the sprint is not affected
worksim.explain: Hire and Develop the Best plus Earn Trust. Help them build capability rather than reporting them or doing the work for them.

worksim.scenario: Your manager asks for a solution to a vague requirement: 'make onboarding faster'. No metric, no scope.
options: Start building the most obvious improvement immediately
Wait for a fully specified ticket
Identify the riskiest assumption, propose a measurable definition of 'faster' and a smallest-useful first slice, confirm it, then start
Design a full re-architecture of onboarding
worksim.explain: Dive Deep plus Invent and Simplify plus Bias for Action. Clarify the highest-risk assumption and move with an explicit, reversible first step rather than either stalling or over-building.

workstyle.a: I prefer to fully validate a plan before acting
workstyle.b: I prefer to act on a reversible decision and adjust as I learn

workstyle.a: I focus deeply on my assigned scope
workstyle.b: I look for problems outside my scope and pick them up

workstyle.a: I make decisions from data I gather myself
workstyle.b: I rely on the judgement of experienced colleagues

workstyle.a: I raise disagreements immediately, even when uncomfortable
workstyle.b: I preserve team harmony and raise concerns privately later

workstyle.a: I prefer detailed instructions before starting
workstyle.b: I prefer an outcome and freedom on the method

workstyle.a: I ship something imperfect and iterate
workstyle.b: I hold a release until quality is high

workstyle.a: I solve problems by digging into details myself
workstyle.b: I solve problems by delegating and coordinating

workstyle.a: I am energised by ambiguous problems
workstyle.b: I am energised by well-defined problems

workstyle.a: I openly share my own mistakes with the team
workstyle.b: I resolve my mistakes quietly and move on
I optimise for shipping the current commitment

workstyle.a: I actively seek feedback that contradicts my view
workstyle.b: I trust my judgement once I have decided

workstyle.a: I do whatever task is needed, including unglamorous work
workstyle.b: I focus on high-leverage technical work
